title: Duration of effects of dietary fish oil supplementation on serum eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid concentrations in dogs

sections.abstract: <jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Objective</jats:title> <jats:p>To determine how long serum concentrations of ω-3 fatty acids remain elevated after cessation of dietary fish oil supplementation.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Animals</jats:title> <jats:p>12 healthy Beagles.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Procedure</jats:title> <jats:p>Baseline serum concentrations of linoleic acid, linolenic acid, arachidonic acid (AA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) were measured. Dogs were then fed a diet supplemented with soybean oil or fish oil for 8 weeks, and serum fatty acid concentrations were measured while dogs were fed the experimental diets and for 18 weeks after they were switched to a maintenance diet.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Results</jats:title> <jats:p>For dogs fed the fish oil diet, serum EPA and DHA concentrations were significantly increased by week 1 and remained increased for 7 (DHA concentration) or 3 (EPA concentration) weeks after dietary fish oil supplementation was discontinued.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title> <jats:p>In dogs, supplementation of the diet with fish oil may have effects for several weeks after dietary supplementation is discontinued.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Clinical Relevance</jats:title> <jats:p>Studies of the effects of fish oil supplementation that use a crossover design should allow for an appropriate washout period. (<jats:italic>Am J Vet Res</jats:italic> 1998;59:864–868)</jats:p> </jats:sec>
